transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-29
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Marcus Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Park (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Icarus - Head of ML), Ben Torres (Icarus - SRE Lead), Lena Ortiz (Icarus - Product)

Summary (auto): Quick reprioritization on what constitutes an apples-to-apples run; agreed to focus on: identical prompt sets, same tokenization, deterministic sampling (greedy/top-k fixed) for latency/throughput runs, and clearly instrumented KV cache warmup steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Marcus: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:10] Aisha: Hi, Aisha here.
[00:12] Ben: Ben, SRE.
[00:14] Lena: Lena for product.
[00:16] Priya: Priya, SE at Redwood. Marcus on the call. Jordan also here.
[00:20] Marcus: Great. We wanted today to be a practical run-through of our benchmarking protocol so you can reproduce numbers on prem and we can compare apples to apples across Hosted/Dedicated.
[00:35] Aisha: Yes, high priority. We ran some naive tests last month and the numbers were all over the place — couldn't tell if it was our batching or the KV being cold.
[00:45] Priya: Totally. That's the usual. We'll walk through prompt set design, load profiles, KV warmup, and then the quant settings.
[01:05] Ben: Quick question up front — for VPC deployment, we will have constrained network egress, so any recommended local caching?
[01:20] Jordan: Yeah, if you're on Private/Dedicated, Redwood supports an in-process KV shim to reduce cross-host KV lookups. We'll show instrumentation points so you can measure hit vs miss rates.
[01:40] Marcus: Okay, agenda — 1) define "workload" (prompt templates + token distributions), 2) define load generator (steady vs spiky), 3) KV cache protocol (warmup + measurement), 4) batching experiments and tail latency, 5) quantization toggles.
[02:05] Priya: Starting with prompt sets: we recommend a mix — 60% short completion (<32 tokens), 30% medium (32-128), 10% long (>128). Use the exact tokenized inputs across runs — not just raw text. We provide a tokenization export script.
[02:30] Aisha: About tokenization — we saw 1–2 token variance between our tokenizer vs the open tokenizer. That changed throughput by a little.
[02:45] Priya: That's expected. So step one: commit to a single tokenizer binary and version. We'll include the tokenizer hash in the run meta.
[03:00] Ben: For the KV cache, how many prefixes should be prefilled? Our production mix has a heavy tail of rare prefixes.
[03:15] Priya: Good question. Our protocol recommends two phases: cold run (no KV warm) to measure worst-case, then a warm run with a synthetic workload that pre-populates the cache to a target hit rate — e.g., aim for 70-80% hit rate for conversational LLMs. We'll include a warmup script that simulates realistic session reuse.
[03:40] Marcus: Also measure effective cache size: instrument key count, average entry size, and eviction rate during the run. Those metrics are important for capacity planning.
[03:55] Lena: Do you have a recommended metric format? We push to Prometheus.
[04:05] Jordan: Yep — we'll push a sample exporter. Metric names: redwood_kv_hit_total, redwood_kv_miss_total, redwood_kv_evictions_total, redwood_batch_size_histogram. We'll send the exporter and a Grafana dashboard.
[04:25] Aisha: Perfect.
[04:30] Priya: Next, load generation. Two canonical profiles: steady-state and burst. Steady-state = constant qps sustained for 10-15 minutes to stabilize batching behavior. Burst = sudden 10–20x spike for 30–120s to exercise autoscaling/fallbacks. For reproducibility use fixed inter-arrival time or Poisson depending on the pattern.
[05:00] Ben: For Poisson vs fixed — our traffic is bursty; should we prefer Poisson to be realistic?
[05:12] Priya: Use Poisson for realistic user arrival; but for controlled bench runs use fixed rates too so you can isolate batching thresholds. We'll provide both templates.
[05:28] Marcus: Important note: seed the random generator and log seeds so you can exactly reproduce the request ordering.
[05:40] Aisha: On sampling/determinism: for throughput/latency runs do you recommend greedy decode?
[05:48] Priya: Yes — deterministic sampling (greedy or fixed top-k with fixed seed) for perf runs. For quality evaluation, toggles to sampling are fine but keep them separate.
[06:05] Lena: Quantization — we've seen big savings with int8, but worried about correctness/regressions. How do you recommend testing?
[06:18] Jordan: Two-stage approach: first, run microbenchmarks with representative prompt pairs and measure delta on embeddings/logits. Then run a small human eval or automatic metric (perplexity/ROUGE/emb similarity) on ~500 examples. Quantization configs should be explicit in run metadata.
[06:40] Priya: Also record exact kernel backends and cudnn/cuda versions. Quant results vary strongly by kernel.
[06:50] Ben: Regarding batching, what max_batch_size do you usually start with on A100-style nodes?
[06:58] Priya: Start with 8, 16, 32 depending on sequence length. We do sweep of max_batch_size and per-batch timeout (e.g., 2–20ms) to map throughput vs p95 latency. We'll share a sweep script.
[07:20] Marcus: Remember to capture p50/p95/p99, and token/sec, effective tokens per GPU second. Those unit economics metrics are what product teams care about.
[07:35] Aisha: For the warmup step, how many streams do you run? One per CPU core? Icarus runs a lot of concurrent sessions.
[07:45] Priya: Warmup should mirror session concurrency distribution. If you have 1k concurrent sessions in production, you don't need to warm that many for bench runs; instead aim to warm working set — the distinct prefix space you expect. Our warmup script takes a target hit-rate and grows the cache until hit-rate stabilizes.
[08:05] Ben: Are there behaviours where batching hides KV misses because of coalescing?
[08:12] Jordan: Yes, coalescing can mask misses. That's why instrument at both request and kernel level. Look at redwood_kv_miss_total AND per-request latency breakdown — if requests that missed the KV show higher generation latency, you'll see the impact.
[08:30] Marcus: We should also talk about network variability for VPC. Packet drops or tail latencies will impact p99 even if client-side machines are fast. For Private deployments, run a network emulator to introduce latency profiles.
[08:50] Aisha: We'll set up tc/netem scenarios for the bench.
[08:55] Priya: Perfect. Now, apples-to-apples: checklist we propose to include in each run meta.json — tokenizer version, model hash, model-variant config (quant), kernel backend, hardware type, power governor, batch config, warmup steps, seed.
[09:20] Lena: Does Redwood provide a canonical meta schema?
[09:25] Marcus: Yes — we'll share a JSON schema.
[09:28] Priya: Moving on to example run: I want to step through an end-to-end. We'll do 1) export tokens, 2) start exporter, 3) run cold test 3 minutes 4) run warmup until 75% hit 5) run steady-state 15 minutes 6) collect metrics.
[10:00] Ben: How do we measure effective token parallelism if you have multiple models served on the same GPU?
[10:10] Jordan: Either isolate a GPU for the run or use tenant tagging in the exporter so you can slice metrics per model. Collocated workloads will interfere; for apples-to-apples you need isolation.
[10:25] Aisha: Isolation is doable in our env for the bench.
[10:30] Priya: Now some gotchas: 1) quantization sometimes reduces kv cache effectiveness if weights are smaller and kernels change; watch accuracy. 2) Batching with dynamic sequence lengths leads to padding overhead — include the token distribution in results. 3) Autoscaling introduces cold-container penalties. Log container start times.
[11:00] Marcus: We also recommended measuring cost-per-response: map GPU-hours and tokens to $/1000-requests; that is part of Redwood Optimize recommendations.
[11:15] Lena: One more practical: can Redwood run a pilot on our VPC? We need to see the Dedicated agent in our subnet.
[11:25] Marcus: Yes — Dedicated pilot is an offering. We'll need a network handshake, customer firewall open list, and an infra window. We'll put specifics in the follow-up.
[11:40] Ben: Security — we need to ensure KMS integration with our HSM for keys used on private. Any docs?
[11:48] Jordan: Yes, we'll share the KMS/HSM integration doc. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and HSM-backed key wrapping.
[12:05] Aisha: Can we get the sample dashboards you mentioned?
[12:10] Priya: Yes. Grafana, Prometheus exporters and a runbook. I'll attach links in the follow-up.
[12:20] Marcus: Quick demo — Priya, can you share your screen to show the sweep script?
[12:32] Priya: (screen share) This is a nodejs/python hybrid loadgen. Key flags: --arrival-model (fixed|poisson), --seed, --max-threads, --profile (warm|cold), --target-qps. Sample profile files define token distributions and prefix lists.
[13:00] Aisha: Nice. That helps.
[13:05] Ben: On instrumentation, what about cost reporting? We prefer per-request token counts included in traces.
[13:12] Jordan: We emit request token counts in trace metadata. Also include per-request breakdown: kv_lookup_time, scheduling_delay, model_inference_time, decode_time.
[13:30] Marcus: If we want to compare Redwood hosted vs your Dedicated nodes, ensure matching kernel backends. We'll provide a matrix of recommended kernels to align.
[13:45] Priya: For reference, we'll include a canonical benchmark spreadsheet with tabs: raw samples, tokenized lengths, run metadata, metrics. We'll also include example graphs (throughput vs max_batch, p95 vs batch_timeout).
[14:05] Lena: Will the benchmarking scripts run inside our CI? We want repeatable nightly runs.
[14:12] Marcus: Yes — scripts are CLI-friendly and can be run inside runners. We recommend tagging runs and storing artifacts (metrics + run meta) in an S3 or internal artifact store.
[14:28] Aisha: One policy question — when you run Dedicated pilot, do you retain logs? We need to ensure log retention policies conform to our regs.
[14:38] Marcus: For pilot, logs are configurable; by default Redwood keeps audit logs for 30 days, but enterprise can extend retention. For Private they can be pushed to customer-managed storage.
[15:00] Ben: Any final tips for the bench?
[15:05] Priya: Start small and iterate. First run: cold vs warm delta and one quant toggle. Second run: batching sweep. Third: burst/scale test. Keep everything in run meta.
[15:18] Jordan: We'll also provide a small test harness for automated comparison across model variants.
[15:25] Marcus: Let's capture next steps — Priya will drop the load scripts and dashboards, Marcus will send pilot pricing and contract skeleton, Ben will provide your actual target qps and p95/p99 numbers.
[15:40] Aisha: Sounds good. Appreciate the clear checklist.
[15:44] Marcus: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links.

Recap / Close:
[16:00] Marcus: Summary: agreement on canonical tokenizer/version, seed determinism, explicit warmup phase for KV, two load patterns (steady + burst), quantization validation steps, and isolation for apples-to-apples runs. Redwood to provide exporter, load scripts, and JSON schema. Icarus to provide targets and infra window.
[16:30] Lena: We'll aim to have the infra window week of 2025-11-10 and Ben will own the p99 target export.
[16:45] Marcus: Great — we'll schedule the 2-hour bench and share invites. Thanks all.

References / Links mentioned:
